# glfx.js — the upstream source and the published build behind `app/vendor/glfx.js`

`app/vendor/glfx.js` carries a copyright header and nothing else identifying it:
no version, no commit, no source map. glfx.js has no releases and no tags, and
the file is not in the upstream repository at all — it is generated by
`build.py` from `src/` and ignored by upstream's own `.gitignore` (`/glfx.js`,
versed below). So the corresponding source for this file is two things, and both
are here:

- `upstream/` — the source tree `build.py` reads, at the commit it was read from.
- `published/glfx.js` — the artifact upstream publishes, which the shipped file
  matches line for line apart from one header line.

Scope: glfx.js only. CamanJS is in `../camanjs/`.

## Pinned upstream

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Repository | <https://github.com/evanw/glfx.js> |
| Releases / tags | none — glfx.js is not published as a package or a versioned release |
| Source commit | `58841c23919bd59787effc0333a4897b43835412` — "add support for OES_texture_float_linear with polyfill", 2013-07-29 |
| Licence | MIT, `upstream/LICENSE` |
| Published artifact | `published/glfx.js`, from branch `gh-pages` at `1bf5f4ec7dfbd039da81d254fb1874cbb0e88228` ("https", 2022-01-10), 28,344 B, git blob `5f812a18dbb868a8dbb2db0ff2336dbbf925eeae` |

Two commits, because the source and the artifact live on different branches and
were last touched nine years apart, not because the pin is loose:
`58841c23919` is the last commit to change `src/` before the 2022 commit that
changed only URLs, and the published artifact is a `gh-pages` file rebuilt
alongside it.

## The shipped file is that artifact, one header line apart

| File | Bytes | Blob / hash |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/vendor/glfx.js` as shipped | 28,403, 59 CRLF | sha256 `68926beb1c83cf8eeaf9ff8e61030158ea27ca0bcfcd6028829a6fca2daa47a1` |
| the same file after CRLF→LF | 28,344 | git blob `f8f29ba7ef06f87a20797620862504f735fb5cc6`, sha256 `68869b90c50a54e9e5c0c76c575fef3da62cfd7a91b4a96dfff099473d30065c` |
| `published/glfx.js` (gh-pages `1bf5f4e`) | 28,344 | git blob `5f812a18dbb868a8dbb2db0ff2336dbbf925eeae`, sha256 `14332d2b292a59e07d2cd3f86bf7e3baa4774a39fcc6ab36c0cba41532657ac3` |

28,403 − 28,344 = 59, the carriage-return count, so the line endings account for
the size difference exactly. After that, the two files differ on **one line**,
line 3, the header URL:

```text
 * http://evanw.github.com/glfx.js/     <- what this app ships
 * https://evanw.github.io/glfx.js/     <- what upstream publishes today
```

Setting the published artifact's header line to the shipped one reproduces the
shipped file byte for byte — same length, same sha256, same git blob
`f8f29ba7`. That substitution is what `verify.mjs` asserts, not a claim in prose.

For completeness of the chain, `deepfriedmemes.com` at
`55db6d6bea0007a6b016102eb5d1ad119bc50ca2` stores `vendor/glfx.js` at blob
`f8f29ba7ef06f87a20797620862504f735fb5cc6` — the same file as here, so this app's
copy is also exactly the original project's copy.

## Why the header says GitHub.com, and why that is not an edit

`build.py` writes the header, from a `header` string literal at the top of the
file. At the pinned commit that literal is the `http://evanw.github.com` form;
the 2022 commit (`86ae72a`, "https") changed that literal, plus the same URL
where it appears in comments and demo pages. A build made before 2022 therefore
stamps the legacy line, and the file this app ships is such a build: the string
is the pinned build tool's own output, not something someone changed here.

`verify.mjs` enforces that reading directly — `upstream/build.py` must contain
the legacy line exactly once and the current line zero times — so a future
"correction" of the header would be caught as an error rather than accepted as a
tidy-up.

## What the build does

`upstream/build.py` is 2,070 bytes and does three things:

1. `sources()` walks `src/` and collects every `.js` file, so the file list is
   whatever is on disk — there is no manifest to fall out of date.
2. `compile()` joins them into `var fx = (function() {\nvar exports = {}; ...`,
   each file preceded by a `// src/path` marker.
3. With `release` in `sys.argv` it pipes that through `os.system('closure --js …')`
   and then compresses GLSL string literals; finally it prepends the header and
   writes `glfx.js`.

**The release path was taken for the artifact that shipped.** Two markers say so:
the published file carries single-letter identifiers, and it carries none of the
`// src/…` markers `compile()` inserts. Both are asserted.

**Nothing was built here.** No `python`, no Closure Compiler, no package install,
no network fetch beyond the two `git` clones this source was read from. That is
also why the artifact is pinned as a file rather than described as reproducible:
`build.py` invokes whatever `closure` is on `PATH`, and neither the compiler nor
its version is recorded anywhere upstream, so the bytes cannot be re-derived from
the tree alone. The published artifact is the reference; the source is what
explains it.

## Source completeness

glfx exports exactly two names, `exports.canvas` and `exports.splineInterpolate`.
Everything else is internal, and the whole public surface is built inside
`exports.canvas`, which attaches methods to the canvas by name:

```js
canvas.bulgePinch = wrap(bulgePinch);
```

The compiler keeps property names, so each attached name survives into the
published artifact while the function behind it may be renamed. That gives a
two-way check, and both directions are clean:

- **29 `.js` files** under `src/` are vendored, plus `build.py`, `LICENSE`,
  `README.md` and `.gitignore`.
- **28 methods are attached** — 6 core (`texture`, `draw`, `update`, `replace`,
  `contents`, `getPixelArray`) and 22 filters. All 28 appear as properties in the
  published artifact, and all 28 backing functions are declared in the vendored
  sources. Nothing in the artifact lacks source; nothing in the source is missing
  from the artifact.

This is the surface the app actually uses: `app/app.js` calls `fx.canvas()` at
line 227 and `bulgePinch` on the result at line 260, with a guard that throws if
`fx.canvas` is not a function.

## Line endings

Upstream is LF. The app's copy is CRLF: 59 line breaks, all 59 CRLF, no lone LF.
`.gitattributes` marks `app/vendor/**` as `-text`, so git normalises nothing
there and the CRLF form is the one the tree holds. Same origin and same advice as
the CamanJS folder: do not "fix" it to LF, and `verify.mjs` refuses that change
because it is a change to the shipped bytes.

## Licence

`upstream/LICENSE` is the MIT text from the pinned commit, 1,059 B, blob
`d8703df912eff879f9d3fad7ece4a073f3a77009`, reproduced verbatim. The notice
agrees on every point it could disagree on: `app/vendor/NOTICE` reproduces this
licence body in full, and its copyright line reads `Copyright (C) 2011 by Evan
Wallace`, character for character the same as the pinned `LICENSE`. The shipped
file also carries its own header naming the same holder and the MIT licence, so
for this library the notice appears in both places.

## Verification

```sh
node third_party/glfx/verify.mjs
```

Offline, dependency-free, no git. Exit 0 prints the chain; exit 1 names the
assertion that broke. It checks the shipped bytes and sha256, the CRLF count, the
CRLF→LF size, sha256 and blob id, the published artifact's sha256 and blob id,
that exactly one line differs and which line it is, that the header substitution
reproduces the shipped file, that `build.py` writes the legacy header and not the
current one, that upstream's `.gitignore` lists the generated file, that the
artifact carries no build path markers, and the 28-method completeness surface in
both directions.

Proven able to fail before it was trusted, on three throwaway copies:

| Control | Result |
| --- | --- |
| one byte flipped inside the shipped bundle | exit 1 — shipped sha256, normalised sha256 and blob id diverge |
| the published artifact's header URL replaced with a third value | exit 1 — published size, sha256 and blob id diverge, then the header assertions |
| `swirl.js` deleted from the vendored sources | exit 1 — 33 files, and `swirl` has no function behind it |

The second control matters most: it changes the reference instead of the artifact,
and the check still fails, so it cannot be satisfied by two files agreeing only
because one of them was moved.

## Deliberately not included

The pinned tree holds 60 files. The manifest above lists 33 of them — the four
root files and all 29 under `src/` — plus the one `gh-pages` artifact. The other
27 are the demo site and the browser tests, none of which is an input to
`glfx.js`, so they are recorded by group instead of vendored:

| Group    | Files | Bytes   | Why not                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|----------|-------|---------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `www/`   | 15    | 631,507 | The documentation and demo site: `www/build.py` (blob `ab202e8e61b9794c3f0e159dfff52717be2ab333`) renders Jinja templates and copies the built `glfx.js` into the site; `www/docs.py` (blob `e6b7abf1d41b8b4f009d03bc2cc86ad54db26163`) generates its docs from `@filter` annotations. Neither writes the library. |
| `tests/` | 12    | 944,265 | Browser pages plus their media — `image.jpg`, `yosemite.jpg`, `cs224.jpg`, `movie.ogg`, `transparent.png` — that exercise the built file in a browser. No build input.                                                                                                                                             |

`www/` is worth naming explicitly because it also contains a `build.py`: that one
is the site builder, not the library builder, and reaching for it by mistake would
produce a docs folder instead of a bundle.

Also upstream, and not sources of this artifact: `gh-pages` carries the published
`glfx.js` that `published/` copies, alongside the same demo assets under
`media/`.
